title: Episode 145: Rutherford B. Hayes and the Stolen Election of 1876: The Wormley Hotel Bargain
description:
In November 1876, the United States stood on the precipice of a second civil war. Democratic candidate Samuel J. Tilden won the national popular vote by a quarter-million ballots and stood just one single electoral vote shy of the presidency. Yet twenty electoral votes across Florida, Louisiana, South Carolina, and Oregon were contested amid allegations of widespread white supremacist terror, ballot stuffing, and fraud. With armed Democratic rifle clubs threatening to march on Washington and swear Tilden in at gunpoint, an emergency fifteen-member Electoral Commission and a midnight backroom bargain at the Wormley Hotel handed the presidency to Rutherford B. Hayes by a single vote: 185 to 184. Discover the high-stakes intrigue that concluded the Reconstruction era.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the most bitterly disputed presidential election in American history—the Centennial Election of 1876. With two rival governments claiming power in three Southern states and the nation staring into the abyss of armed insurrection, leaders met in a smoke-filled suite at Washington's Wormley Hotel to forge a fateful pact that seated Rutherford B. Hayes and ended Reconstruction. Here is George with the full story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: ELECTION NIGHT IN COLUMBUS
On the evening of Tuesday, November 7, 1876, Governor Rutherford B. Hayes sat by the fireside in the executive mansion in Columbus, Ohio, reading incoming telegraph dispatches with mounting sorrow. The nation had celebrated its centennial summer with great patriotic expositions in Philadelphia, but the political mood across the country was dark and vengeful. Exhausted by eight years of economic depression following the Panic of 1873, and disgusted by scandals in the Grant administration, Northern voters had turned sharply toward the Democratic Party. The Democratic nominee, Governor Samuel J. Tilden of New York—the wealthy, cerebral crusader who had smashed the corrupt Tweed Ring—had swept New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, and Indiana.

By midnight, every major newspaper in the country, including the staunchly Republican New York Tribune, had conceded the presidency to Tilden. Hayes turned to his wife Lucy, smiled faintly, and said softly: 'Well, Lucy, I believe we are beaten. But I hope the country will be safe in Mr. Tilden's hands.' Hayes went to bed convinced his political career was over. Tilden had captured 184 electoral votes—exactly one vote shy of the 185 required for victory. He led Hayes by over two hundred and fifty thousand popular votes. But in the pre-dawn darkness of New York City, a frantic visitor knocked on the door of the Republican National Committee at the Fifth Avenue Hotel, carrying a realization that would throw the republic into chaos.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE PRE-DAWN PLOT OF DAN SICKLES AND 'DEVIL DICK'
At three o'clock in the morning on November 8, General Daniel E. Sickles—the notorious Union general who had lost a leg at Gettysburg—limped into Republican headquarters on crutches. Finding Chairman Zachariah Chandler asleep and drunk with despair, Sickles began scrutinizing the telegraph tape. He noticed an extraordinary anomaly: the Democratic state committee in Florida had telegraphed the New York World asking for telegrams confirming Tilden's victory, admitting Florida was too close to call. Sickles realized instantly that if Hayes could sweep every single remaining uncertified electoral vote in Florida, South Carolina, Louisiana, and one disputed elector in Oregon—twenty electoral votes in total—Hayes would reach exactly 185 votes and win the presidency by a margin of one.

Without waiting for party permission, Sickles drafted frantic telegrams to Republican governors and election officials in Tallahassee, New Orleans, and Columbia: 'With your state, Hayes is elected. Do not concede a single precinct. Hold your state at all costs.' At dawn, Chandler awoke, rubbed his eyes, and issued his immortal, defiant press bulletin to the nation: 'Hayes has 185 electoral votes and is elected.' The Democratic Party erupted in fury, accusing Republicans of attempting to steal the election in broad daylight. Both parties dispatched teams of prominent 'visiting statesmen'—lawyers, senators, and political operatives—armed with carpetbags filled with cash to monitor the Southern returning boards.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE CRUCIBLE OF THE RETURNING BOARDS
The situation on the ground in the three disputed Southern states was a nightmare of competing frauds and rampant racial terror. In South Carolina, Louisiana, and Florida, the remaining Republican state administrations were kept in power only by the presence of federal troops. In counties across the Red River Valley of Louisiana and the Upcountry of South Carolina, armed Democratic rifle clubs and White Leagues had conducted a systematic campaign of terror, assassinating Black Republican leaders and blockading polling places to prevent freedmen from voting. In parishes where Black voters outnumbered white voters three to one, local tallies showed unanimous Democratic majorities.

In response, the Republican-dominated State Returning Boards exercised sweeping statutory powers to throw out ballots from precincts where intimidation and violence had occurred. In Louisiana alone, the board invalidated over thirteen thousand Democratic votes, transforming Tilden's initial six-thousand-vote lead into a four-thousand-vote victory for Hayes. In Florida, competing canvassers certified opposing tallies. When the Electoral College met on December 6, two competing slates of electoral certificates—one signed by Republican officials for Hayes, the other signed by Democratic officials for Tilden—were submitted to Congress from all three states. The United States Constitution provided that the President of the Senate should open the certificates in the presence of both houses, but remained completely silent on who possessed the authority to decide between conflicting sets of returns.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE THREAT OF CIVIL WAR AND THE FIFTEEN-MEMBER COMMISSION
As January 1877 dawned, the nation drifted toward catastrophe. The House of Representatives was controlled by Democrats; the Senate was controlled by Republicans. Neither house would yield. House Democrats threatened to use procedural filibusters to block the counting of electoral votes past March 4, leaving the country without a president and precipitating a constitutional vacuum. Across the South, Confederate veterans began drilling in open fields; in the North, Democratic newspapers carried headlines screaming 'Tilden or Blood!' and urged a hundred thousand armed men to march on Washington to install Tilden in the Executive Mansion. President Grant quietly reinforced the military garrison in Washington, stationing artillery at the arsenal and posting cavalry detachments around the Capitol.

Recognizing that armed conflict was imminent, moderate leaders in Congress forged a compromise in late January, establishing an extraordinary emergency tribunal: the Electoral Commission of 1877. The commission consisted of fifteen members: five senators (three Republicans, two Democrats), five representatives (three Democrats, two Republicans), and five Supreme Court justices. Four justices were pre-selected—two Republicans and two Democrats—who were instructed to select the fifth justice. That decisive fifth member was intended to be Justice David Davis of Illinois, an independent-minded jurist who was respected by both parties as an impartial umpire.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE BLUNDER OF DAVID DAVIS AND THE 8-TO-7 COURT
Just as the compromise bill passed, Illinois Democrats committed one of the most astonishing political blunders in American history. Hoping to curry favor with Justice Davis and guarantee his vote for Tilden on the Commission, a coalition of Democrats and Greenbackers in the Illinois state legislature elected Davis to the United States Senate. The Democrats expected Davis to remain on the Commission as a senator or vote for Tilden before taking his Senate seat. Instead, Davis—a man of rigid judicial propriety—was offended by the crass political maneuver and immediately resigned from both the Supreme Court and the Electoral Commission entirely.

With Davis gone, the four remaining justices were forced to select an alternate from the Supreme Court bench. Every remaining justice was a Republican. They chose Justice Joseph P. Bradley of New Jersey, a cerebral, highly legalistic jurist. When the Commission convened in the Supreme Court chamber in February, attorneys argued for days over whether the Commission had the power to 'go behind the returns' to investigate fraud and violence, or whether it was bound to accept the official certification of state governors. On February 9, by a strict party-line vote of 8 to 7, Justice Bradley voted with his fellow Republicans, establishing the rule that the Commission would not go behind the state certifications. One by one, Florida, Louisiana, South Carolina, and Oregon were awarded to Rutherford B. Hayes by the identical, agonizing margin: 8 to 7.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: MIDNIGHT AT THE WORMLEY HOTEL
With the Commission ruling 8 to 7 on every contest, infuriated Democrats in the House launched a crippling filibuster in late February, vowing to prevent the certification before Grant's term expired at noon on March 4. In desperation, Hayes's closest political allies—including Ohio Congressman Charles Foster and future President James A. Garfield—convened secret late-night negotiating sessions with influential Southern Democrats in Room 118 of the Wormley Hotel in Washington, owned by James Wormley, a wealthy African American businessman.

The terms of the historic 'Compromise of 1877' were hammered out over glasses of bourbon. Southern Democrats agreed to drop the filibuster, allow the electoral count to proceed to completion, and permit Hayes to be peacefully inaugurated. In exchange, Hayes's representatives pledged that upon taking office, President Hayes would withdraw all remaining federal troops from the statehouses of South Carolina and Louisiana, effectively ending federal military protection of Reconstruction state governments. Furthermore, Hayes promised to appoint a Southern Democrat to his cabinet and support substantial federal funding for Southern internal improvements, including the Texas and Pacific Railway. The deal was struck: the South conceded the White House in exchange for home rule and the abandonment of federal enforcement of civil rights.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE MIDNIGHT OATH AND THE LONG SHADOW OF 1877
At 4:10 AM on the morning of March 2, 1877, just forty-four hours before Grant's term expired, the President of the Senate formally announced the final electoral tally: Rutherford B. Hayes, 185; Samuel J. Tilden, 184. Because March 4 fell on a Sunday, and fearing that an armed uprising or injunction might be served before Monday's public ceremonies, President Grant arranged for Hayes to take the oath of office in absolute secrecy on Saturday evening, March 3, in the Red Room of the White House before a small gathering of cabinet members. Hayes repeated the oath, kissed the Bible, and legally became President forty-eight hours before anyone outside the building knew.

On April 24, 1877, fulfilling the Wormley agreement, President Hayes ordered federal soldiers stationed at the New Orleans Cabildo and the Columbia statehouse to return to their barracks. Deprived of military protection, the last Republican Reconstruction governments instantly collapsed, and conservative white Democrats seized total control of the South. Hayes was derided by bitter Democrats as 'His Fraudulency' and 'Rutherfraud B. Hayes,' while Black citizens felt utterly betrayed by a nation that had traded their hard-won constitutional protections for political peace. The Compromise of 1877 averted a second civil war, but it ushered in seven decades of Jim Crow segregation and disenfranchisement across the American South.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The disputed election of 1876 tested the American constitutional framework almost to destruction. Rutherford B. Hayes assumed the presidency under a cloud of controversy, yet he would govern with remarkable personal integrity, battling corruption in his own party. Next week, we examine Hayes's domestic battles: his war against the New York political machine and the famous temperance regime of his first lady, 'Lemonade Lucy.' Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
